newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal BCI aims for break-even in 1996.
newsitem.headline: Portugal BCI aims for break-even in 1996.

text.p: Portugal's Banco de Comercio e Industria (BCI) hopes a dramatic change in its strategy will allow it to break even on the operating side in 1996, BCI president Joao Costa Pinto said.
"We're aiming for an operational break-even at the end of 1996," Costa Pinto told Reuters in an interview, adding that this year's nine-month results indicated the bank would achieve its goal.
"Given the profound change in our strategy and medium-term goals, we expect that BCI will begin a clear process of financial recovery from 1997," he said.
BCI, whose major shareholders are the Banco Santander and Royal Bank of Scotland groups, made a loss of 1.85 billion escudos in 1995.
In the first half of this year it made a consolidated net profit of 84.40 million escudos.

"In recent years BCI has had to resolve a lot of problems which resulted from its previous, less successful strategy of rapid growth", Costa Pinto said, adding that 1996 would be a year for internal reorganisation and consolidation.
"The new strategy, recently approved by shareholders, aims at turning BCI into a medium-sized, high-tech institution which will be able to offer high quality services," he said.
By the end of the transition period, BCI hopes to have 140 branches, up from 102 at present, and to have doubled its market share to four percent.
Costa Pinto said the bank's two principal shareholders would help it to develop new technologies such as telephone and electronic banking and home banking.
"Portuguese banking has undergone radical changes as a result of acquisitions and privatisations and the banks are making a big effort to modernise and reorganise," he noted.
"Against this background we had to change our old strategy of quick growth."
BCI is particularly keen to use new technology to cash in on increasing cross-border financial deals between Portugal and Spain.
Costa Pinto said the few BCI shares that remained on the Lisbon bourse since the Santander group took a controlling stake would probably cease trading soon.
Slightly more than five percent of the bank's total share capital of 31.12 billion escudos is quoted on the bourse.
"The performance of BCI's shares during the reorganisation has not been good for the image of the bank," he said.
"Given the small percentage of capital not held by the strategic shareholders, the board decided it would be preferable to take the shares off the bourse."
Shareholders will vote on the proposal at the next general assembly on November 29.
